CHI Internship: SAR Systems Integration Practicum, Technical Report 02

**SAR Integration Test 02: TouchDesigner-to-QLab OSC Return Path**

*Confirming That TouchDesigner Can Command QLab over the Same Link*

**Gabriel A. Aguilar**  
Center for Holistic Integration (CHI), Self-Aware Room (SAR)  
CUNY New York City College of Technology, Brooklyn, NY

October 8, 2026

**Abstract**

A conversation needs two voices, and Test 01 only proved one of them. This report documents the second integration test of the Self-Aware Room (SAR) show-control pipeline, which reverses the direction of the link. Using the same network as Test 01, a TouchDesigner OSC Out DAT sent QLab’s native command /cue/ACK/name to QLab’s listening port, 53000, and QLab renamed a Memo cue numbered ACK to “Hello from TD.” Together with Test 01, this shows that OSC can travel in both directions over a single Ethernet cable. Five issues came up along the way: an indentation error in the Textport, an operator path that could not be found, a mix-up between the OSC Out CHOP and the OSC Out DAT, a QLab permission that depends on another permission, and a suspected firewall block that turned out not to be one. The permission dependency, in which View must be enabled before Edit, is recorded here as a configuration requirement for the SAR standard.

***Keywords:** Open Sound Control, QLab OSC API, TouchDesigner, OSC Out DAT, Bidirectional Show Control, Self-Aware Room*

# **1\. Introduction**

Test 01 (Aguilar, 2026a) established that QLab can select video clips in TouchDesigner over a direct Ethernet link. A handshake, however, needs a reply: TouchDesigner also has to be able to send OSC that QLab will accept and act on. Test 02 isolates that return path by sending one message from TouchDesigner, triggered by hand, and watching for QLab’s response. The success criteria were:

1. TouchDesigner sends an OSC message addressed to QLab over the existing Ethernet link.

2. QLab accepts the message from a client that has no passcode.

3. QLab performs a visible action in response.

For the visible action I chose renaming a cue, since it is easy to see and changes nothing else in the workspace. I numbered the target cue ACK, short for acknowledgment, which is a reply confirming that a message was received; QLab treats it as an ordinary cue number.

# **2\. Materials and Methods**

## ***2.1 Equipment, Software and Network***

The equipment, software, and network addressing were the same as in Test 01 (Table 1). The QLab machine listens for OSC on port 53000, QLab’s default, and the receiving network built in TouchDesigner for Test 01, which listens on port 7000, was left in place.

**Table 1\.** *Network addressing, unchanged across Tests 01 through 03\.*

| Setting | QLab machine (macOS) | TouchDesigner machine |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Ethernet IP | 192.168.10.10 | 192.168.10.20 |
| Subnet mask | 255.255.255.0 | 255.255.255.0 |
| Router / gateway | blank | blank |
| Wi-Fi address | 10.2.215.89 (campus) | campus network |
| OSC listening port | 53000 (QLab default) | 7000 (OSC In CHOP and DAT) |

## ***2.2 QLab Configuration***

I added a Memo cue to the workspace, set its Number field to ACK, and left its name blank. QLab ignores incoming OSC unless the client sending it has permission, and in OSC Access (Workspace Settings, Network) every permission for clients without a passcode started out turned off (Figure 1). Renaming a cue counts as an edit, so I enabled View and Edit for the No Passcode row (Table 2).

![The OSC Access panel in its starting state: Allow OSC connections is on, but View, Edit, and Control are unchecked for clients without a passcode. In this state QLab ignores TouchDesigner.][image1]

**Figure 1\.** *The OSC Access panel in its starting state: Allow OSC connections is on, but View, Edit, and Control are unchecked for clients without a passcode. In this state QLab ignores TouchDesigner.*

**Table 2\.** *QLab settings changed for Test 02\.*

| Setting | Value |
| :---- | :---- |
| ACK cue type | Memo |
| ACK cue Number | ACK |
| Allow OSC connections | On |
| OSC listening port | 53000 (TCP and UDP), default |
| No Passcode permissions | View and Edit checked; View must be checked first |

## ***2.3 TouchDesigner Configuration***

In TouchDesigner, I configured an OSC Out DAT (oscout1) to send to the QLab machine (Figure 2; Table 3). I sent the message by hand from the Textport, opened with Alt+T, using the DAT’s sendOSC method; that method returns the number of bytes it sent, which makes it a quick way to confirm that a message actually left the machine.

![Parameters of the OSC Out DAT oscout1: Messaging (UDP), Network Address 192.168.10.10, Port 53000.][image2]

**Figure 2\.** *Parameters of the OSC Out DAT oscout1: Messaging (UDP), Network Address 192.168.10.10, Port 53000\.*

**Table 3\.** *OSC Out DAT parameters.*

| Parameter | Value |
| :---- | :---- |
| Active | On |
| Protocol | Messaging (UDP) |
| Network Address | 192.168.10.10 (QLab machine, Ethernet) |
| Port | 53000 (QLab OSC listener) |
| Shared Connection | On |

The command I sent was:

op('/project1/oscout1').sendOSC('/cue/ACK/name', \['Hello from TD'\])

/cue/ACK/name belongs to QLab’s own OSC command set; it sets the name of the cue numbered ACK. Because QLab only understands its own commands, this message cannot use the /sar/ namespace. That is to say, any SAR-level message meant for QLab will need to be translated into one of QLab’s native addresses before it is sent.

## ***2.4 Procedure***

1. Add the ACK Memo cue in QLab and enable View, then Edit, for No Passcode clients.

2. Add and configure the OSC Out DAT in TouchDesigner.

3. Run the sendOSC command from the Textport and note the value it returns.

4. Check whether the ACK cue in QLab has been renamed.

# **3\. Results**

The return path worked. Every sendOSC call returned 36, the number of bytes sent, and once the permissions were set, QLab renamed the ACK cue to “Hello from TD” (Figures 3 and 4; Table 4).

![The Textport session. The earlier lines show the errors listed in Table 5; the final four commands, which use the full path /project1/oscout1, each return 36.][image3]

**Figure 3\.** *The Textport session. The earlier lines show the errors listed in Table 5; the final four commands, which use the full path /project1/oscout1, each return 36\.*

![The QLab cue list after the command: the Memo cue numbered ACK now carries the name “Hello from TD.”][image4]

**Figure 4\.** *The QLab cue list after the command: the Memo cue numbered ACK now carries the name “Hello from TD.”*

**Table 4\.** *Results against the success criteria.*

| Check | Result |
| :---- | :---- |
| TouchDesigner sends OSC (36 bytes per send) | Pass |
| QLab accepts commands from an unpasscoded client (View and Edit) | Pass |
| QLab acts on the command (ACK cue renamed) | Pass |
| Return path shares the Test 01 cable, addresses, and Wi-Fi setup | Pass |
| Automated round trip on each GO | Not tested; see Test 03 |

# **4\. Discussion**

## ***4.1 Issues Encountered and Resolutions***

Five issues came up before the test passed (Table 5). Most of them were about finding the right operator or the right checkbox rather than anything wrong with the network; the cable was ready long before the software was.

**Table 5\.** *Issues encountered during Test 02\.*

| Issue | Cause | Resolution |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| IndentationError: unexpected indent in the Textport | Leading spaces before the pasted command | Enter commands flush left |
| 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'sendOSC' | The Textport runs from the root, so op('oscout1') found nothing; guessed names such as oscout2 and oscout3 did not exist | Use the full path /project1/...; list OSC Out DATs with \[o.path for o in op('/').findChildren(type=oscoutDAT)\] |
| 'td.oscoutCHOP' object has no attribute 'sendOSC' | The first operator used was an OSC Out CHOP; only the OSC Out DAT has sendOSC | Use an OSC Out DAT, which has a pink border rather than a green one |
| Edit could not be checked in OSC Access | QLab requires View before Edit or Control can be enabled | Check View first, then Edit |
| Suspected macOS firewall block | Checked in System Settings, Network, Firewall | Firewall was off; ruled out |

## ***4.2 Limitations***

* The message was triggered by hand; the automated reply on each GO is tested separately in Test 03\.

* QLab’s replies, which it sends on port 53001, were not captured, so I judged acceptance only by the visible rename.

* Permissions were granted to every client without a passcode, which is acceptable on an isolated link but not necessarily in production.

## ***4.3 Implications for the SAR Standard***

The permission order in QLab, View before Edit or Control, needs to be part of the documented setup procedure. A fresh workspace ignores incoming commands without saying a word, and anyone who does not know about that dependency could easily lose an afternoon looking for a network problem that does not exist. The SAR OSC Library should also record how /sar/qlab/... messages translate into QLab’s native /cue/... commands.

# **5\. Conclusion and Future Work**

In conclusion, TouchDesigner can send OSC commands that QLab accepts over the same direct Ethernet link used for QLab-to-TouchDesigner control. With Tests 01 and 02 complete, both directions have been proven on their own; the next step is to make them answer each other. The open items are:

* Automate the reply so that each QLab GO produces a full round trip (Test 03).

* Test /cue/ACK/start so TouchDesigner can fire QLab cues; this requires the Control permission.

* Capture QLab’s replies on port 53001 after sending /alwaysReply 1.

* Decide whether production should use a passcode instead of open No Passcode permissions.

* Rename or remove the unused OSC Out CHOP so it is not confused with the DAT.
